item.title: Fast Shape Retrieval Based on Differential Chain Code Descriptor and Fuzzy Contour Matching
item.description:
The problem

Matching a known shape in an image is a basic step in industrial inspection and measurement. Feature-based methods such as SIFT, SURF and ORB describe key points, but they perform poorly under heavy noise, blur or strong viewpoint change, and the many feature points make them computationally intensive. Template-based methods compare image patches directly, which is costly over large search spaces and sensitive to scale, rotation and illumination. This paper therefore matches contours, using the structural and topological information they carry.

A chain code turns a contour into a sequence of direction changes, so two similar shapes produce similar sequences and matching becomes sequence comparison. The catch is that the sequence is ordered: one noise point shifts the correspondence of the points after it, and the longer the code, the more points are misaligned and the larger the error.

How it works

The method first turns each contour into an ordered, evenly spaced point set and encodes it as differential chain codes. It then matches the local contour against the model in short segments, so that a noise point only disturbs the segment it falls in, and finally checks each candidate position geometrically.

  1. Extract, smooth and resample the contour. Run-length encoding of the binary image, a connectivity analysis and a depth-first search give the outer and inner contours, with points about 1 pixel apart. The points are smoothed with the mean of their neighbours and then sampled at a fixed distance, which reduces their number while keeping the shape.
  2. Encode the turning angles. Instead of computing an ordinary chain code first, each point and its two neighbours form two vectors, and the rotation angle between them is quantised into a differential code. The contour becomes a code sequence that does not change when the shape is translated.
  3. Match short segments. The code of the local contour is divided into short segments. Each segment slides along the longer model code, and at every position the cost is the sum of absolute code differences. Each segment produces one cost array as long as the model code.
  4. Combine the costs and pick candidates. A sliding window writes the minimum cost inside the window into its centre, which absorbs small shifts of the best position. The segment cost arrays are then combined into one total cost. The total forms valleys; positions with small cost are kept, and the centre of each valley becomes a candidate starting position.
  5. Verify with SVD. Fuzzy matching can also return look-alike or wrong positions. For each candidate, the local points are paired with the model points, a transformation is estimated by singular value decomposition (SVD), and the mean distance between the transformed pairs scores the match. The positions with the smallest mean distance are kept. An optional ICP step refines the final alignment.

Results

Lower mean distance than Halcon and Smart on all 8 test images: 0.376–0.601 for the proposed method, against 0.694–1.027 for Halcon and 0.642–0.958 for Smart (Table 1).
0.372–0.447 with ICP refinement, with standard deviations of 0.155–0.189, against standard deviations of 0.269–0.483 for Halcon (Table 1).

The test material is CAD drawings captured with the SmartFlash-2020 one-click measurement sensor, an instrument for large flat products with a measurement range of up to 300 × 200 mm. Each original image was rotated clockwise by 30°, 60°, 90°, 120° and 150° and matched against the original, and further experiments test matching under multi-target interference. For the quantitative comparison, Table 1 reports the mean distance and standard deviation between the matched contour and the ground truth on eight test images, for Halcon, a baseline referred to as Smart, the proposed method, and the proposed method followed by ICP.

The proposed method has the lowest mean distance of the three methods on every image; on test image 2, for example, it is 0.426, against 1.027 for Halcon and 0.715 for Smart. ICP refinement lowers the mean distance on seven images and leaves it unchanged on image 6 (0.376), with the largest reductions on images 8, 5 and 4 (0.601 → 0.372, 0.581 → 0.391 and 0.578 → 0.419). As future work, the authors plan more advanced smoothing, an improved fuzzy matching algorithm and the use of deep learning.

item.title: Transformation of LEGO Models
item.description:
The problem

Container stacking raises a practical question: how can containers be moved efficiently from one stack to another? This paper studies a remotely related question with LEGO: build a new LEGO model using bricks taken from an existing one. Many algorithms turn a 3D shape into a LEGO model, but constructing a LEGO model from the bricks of another model had not been explored in open literature. The task has two goals that pull against each other. Every pick-and-place (PnP) of a brick costs one move, and as many bricks of the source model as possible should end up in the target.

Physical constraints make the order of moves matter. A brick fully or partly under other bricks cannot be picked, and a brick cannot be placed where it would hang in the air. The authors also treat a top-surface brick that is completely surrounded by other bricks as not movable, because freeing it would take extra moves.

How it works

The source model is taken apart from the top down and the target is built from the bottom up, layer by layer. Two basic approaches, rigid transformation (RT) and flexible transformation (FT), decide how the target’s bricks are chosen, and three strategies decide where each brick comes from: straight from the source, from a buffer of bricks already removed, or from a stock with an unlimited supply. Combining them gives six algorithms, RT1–RT3 and FT1–FT3, which use seven brick shapes.

  1. Moves and constraints. Each PnP of one brick (source to buffer, source to target, buffer to target or stock to target) counts as a cost of 1. Only movable bricks, those with nothing on top and not fully surrounded, can be picked.
  2. Rigid or flexible target. In rigid transformation (RT), the target LEGO model is generated before the transformation, with large bricks used first on each layer. In flexible transformation (FT), the target is built from an interim voxelized model on the fly: a scoring rule weights each brick type by how many movable bricks of that type the source currently offers, so source bricks are used first.
  3. Strategy 1. The source is disassembled completely into the buffer, and the target is built from the buffer, with the stock filling in bricks the buffer lacks.
  4. Strategy 2. Movable source bricks go straight to the target. If none matches, the buffer is searched; if it has none either, one more layer of the source is disassembled into the buffer to uncover new bricks. The stock is used only when the source is gone.
  5. Strategy 3. No buffer. A matching movable source brick goes straight to the target; otherwise the stock supplies one.

The algorithms are compared with three metrics: the cost C, the number of PnP needed to build the target; the reuse rate R = Nr/Ns, the share of the source’s Ns bricks that end up in the target; and an overall performance P = V·R/C, where V is the number of voxels in the target model.

Results

FT3 gives the best overall performance of the six algorithms, averaged over all 56 ordered pairs of the eight models, at each of seven model sizes; among the RT algorithms, RT2 is best (Fig. 7c).
Strategies 1 and 2 reach very similar reuse rates, so disassembling the whole source upfront is not worthwhile (Fig. 7b).
Ball to house with colour matching: FT3 reuses 73.0 % of the bricks at 2673 PnP, against 74.8 % at 4502 PnP for FT1 (Fig. 8).

The algorithms were tested on eight triangle mesh models converted to LEGO. In the first test, model A was transformed into each of the other seven models at about 2500 voxels per model. In the second, all eight models were transformed into each other at seven model sizes. Cost grows linearly with model size, and cost drops from Strategy 1 to 2 to 3 at every model size. An FT algorithm costs more than its RT counterpart because FT builds a target with more bricks. FT3 reaches a reuse rate comparable to the best RT algorithms. RT3’s reuse rate is much lower than RT1’s and RT2’s: when the target bricks are fixed in advance and there is no buffer, matching source bricks are hard to find, and on average more than half of the target bricks come from the stock. Reuse rate is not very sensitive to model size above 1700 voxels per model; smaller models reduce it.

The third test added colour: exterior bricks must match the surface colour, while interior bricks may take any colour. For the ball-to-house transformation, RT1 and RT2 reuse 61.9 % and 59.9 % of the bricks, and RT3 only 9.2 % (Fig. 9). The authors note the trade-offs: FT’s higher reuse comes with more and smaller bricks, giving weaker structures with internal sliding planes; the overall performance metric is empirical, and other scenarios may weigh cost differently. The study moves one brick at a time; reusing groups of bricks as modules is left to future work, and the results may not be directly applicable to a specific industrial application such as cargo container stacking.

item.title: Design of LEGO Assembly Transformation
item.description:
This paper presents a design method for LEGO assembly transformation, addressing the problem of reassembling an existing LEGO model into a different target shape while optimizing the use of available bricks. This conference paper presents the foundational design framework that was subsequently extended in the journal version (Computer-Aided Design and Applications, 2018).
